title: What is known about 1RB0RA_0RC0RE_1LD1LF_1LE0LC_1RA0LD_0RA---
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB0RA_0RC0RE_1LD1LF_1LE0LC_1RA0LD_0RA---.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state, two-symbol Turing machine halts when started on a blank tape: it is one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project. This page lists what has been established about it, sorted by what each result rests on.
verdict: The question is open. The tape splits into a small counter at the left end, a register of 331 three-cell digits and a tail of 110 blocks that grows by one block per sweep. The leftward pass over the tail is proved in Lean for every length; the register's dynamics are observed, not understood, and nothing found says whether F can ever read a 1.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (F1); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: The leftward pass over the tail, for every length
claims.text: With a 0 beyond, 0 (110110)^n C> 001 becomes 0 C> 001 (001001)^n in 20n steps, for every n and every tape beyond: the head in C crosses the tail two blocks at a time and rewrites each 110 as 001 (the pass back to the right writes them back). A small generalisation of the shared cross_l lemma (a fixed cell between head and repeats) is proved alongside.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 38,455 cells have been visited and 21,618 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: Growth shape: exp/sqrt
claims.text: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the logarithm of the step count: each new cell costs a roughly constant factor more time, the signature of a counter or of a Collatz-like map whose values are written on the tape (fitted exponent 0.031). Right of the start it grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.462).

claims.title: No halt in 10<sup>10</sup> steps
claims.text: tools/c/tmrun.c runs 1010 steps from blank tape without a halt (42,020 ones at the end).

claims.title: No closed tape language from windows up to 7
claims.text: bbtools.ctl with windows of K = 2 to 7 cells closes but allows F to read a 1 (18 to 1,920 abstract halting configurations). n-gram CPS (widths 3 to 7, with history and LRU augmentations) fails too.

claims.title: Three zones
claims.text: Sampled with the head in A at the right end, the tape is a left counter (runs of 10 such as c^40 0 c^61 a c^17 0 c^3 with c = 10, a = 110), then a register that, cut into three-cell digits from the right, uses only 110 (1) and 010 (0), then the tail (110)^t 1. Since step 764,833 the register has exactly 331 digits; t grows by one every sweep (t = 21,472 at 3·109 steps). Observed to 1010 steps.

claims.title: The register is a counter
claims.text: The left part of the register is still the fresh pattern 1010… it was born with; only a zone at its right (low) end changes, and at every sweep: in 4,244 consecutive sweeps (to 108 steps) the leftmost changed digit was within 20 digits of the end 93% of the time, never more than 60 away. The active zone eats into the fresh part slowly (about 148 fresh digit pairs at 3·106 steps, 136 at 3·109): a counter whose length grows like the logarithm of the number of sweeps. Early on (step 760,470) the tail, then 329 blocks long, was absorbed into the register, which grew from 12 to 331 digits.

claims.title: Does it halt?
claims.text: Not known. The only halt is F on a 1; F is entered from C reading a 1 (about 4% of steps) and has always read a 0, mostly with 1011 to its left. A halt would have to come from the counter in the register or the left-end counter, whose rules are not known.

explainer.lede: Nobody knows. Started on a blank tape, this Turing machine has run for 10<sup>9</sup> steps without stopping. This page runs the real machine in your browser, shows the shape of its run, and lists what is known, each result marked by what it rests on.

facts.text: No halt in the C simulator; 38,455 cells visited.
No halt, proved in Lean; the first 10,000 by the kernel alone.

sections.eyebrow: What the tape is made of
sections.heading: A counter, a register and a tail
html: Each time the head reaches the right end in state A the tape looks like this (step 2,997,000; c = 10, a = 110, d = 110010):
c^40 0 c^61 a c^17 0 c^3 | d^148 0 c 0 c d 0 c 0 c d a^4 d 0 c 0 c 0 c a d 0 c 0 c d^2 0 c d^3 0 c | a^571 1 A>

On the left a few runs of 10: a small counter that changes only at rare moments. In the middle a register: cut into three-cell digits from the right it uses only 110 (read as 1) and 010 (read as 0). In this sample it reads

sections.heading: The tail grows by one block per sweep
html: The head bounces between the right end and the register. Going left over the tail it rewrites every 110 as 001, two blocks per 20 steps (proved in Lean for every length: 0 (110110)^n C> 001 → 0 C> 001 (001001)^n); it then does some work at the right end of the register, comes back writing the 110s again, and adds one block at the end. So the tail length counts the sweeps, and the right side grows like the square root of the step count.

sections.heading: The register is a slowly growing counter
html: The register has had exactly 331 digits since step 764,833, when the tail of the time (329 blocks) was swallowed into it. Its left part is still the fresh 1010… pattern; each sweep changes only digits near its right end, like the low digits of a counter being stepped. Five consecutive sweeps near step 108 end the register with

The changed zone eats into the fresh part very slowly (a few digits per factor 10 of time), which is the shape of a counter: the left end of the tape is reached ever more rarely, and the left side grows like a logarithm.

sections.heading: Open, and not yet reduced
html: The machine halts only if F reads a 1. F is entered after C reads a 1 and has always found a 0. The tail and the passes are regular and cannot produce the halt; whether the register counter or the left counter can ever bring F onto a 1 is the question, and their rules are not known yet, so no reduction to a number-theoretic question is given here.

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the logarithm of the step count: each new cell costs a roughly constant factor more time, the signature of a counter or of a Collatz-like map whose values are written on the tape (fitted exponent 0.031). Right of the start it grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.462).
After 109 steps the tape spans 38,455 cells (245 left of the start, 28,256 right), with a density of 1s of 0.562.
These are measurements of one bounded run, sorted by tools/py/bbtools/triage.py; the macro structure behind them is the next thing to find.

summary: A bouncer whose tail of 110 blocks grows by one block per sweep, crossing a fixed register of 331 three-cell digits (110 = 1, 010 = 0) whose low end it rewrites at every pass like a slowly growing counter; a small counter at the far left ticks rarely.
